evidence.text:
OBCFC - Micro-Project Proposal (2025-2026)Division of Computer Science and Engineering
Personalized Learning Platform
1.0  Rationale
Every learner has a different pace, background and set of strengths. Most conventional e-learning
platforms, however, deliver the same fixed sequence of lessons to everyone. Fast learners become
bored, struggling learners fall behind, and revision is left entirely to the student. A personalized
learning platform addresses this gap by adapting the content, the order of topics and the revision
schedule to each learner's actual performance.
Building such a platform is, at its core, a Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) problem. Course
topics and their prerequisites naturally form a directed graph; learning paths can be generated using
graph traversal and topological ordering; the "most urgent topic to revise" can be found efficiently
with a priority queue (heap); topic search and auto-suggestion can be handled by a trie; and learner
records can be stored and retrieved quickly using hash tables and linked structures. Choosing the
right structure directly decides whether the system responds instantly or slows down as the number
of learners and topics grows.
This micro-project is therefore significant for three reasons. First, it applies the syllabus concepts –
linear structures, dynamic structures, searching and sorting, trees and graphs – to a single realistic,
socially useful application instead of isolated exercises. Second, it lets the team evaluate the
performance of different algorithms (for example linear versus binary search, or different sorting
techniques) on real data, which supports the macro-level competency of evaluating application
functionality in various situations. Third, personalized and adaptive learning is a growing need in
education, and a lightweight, well-engineered prototype demonstrates how good algorithmic design
can improve learning outcomes without heavy infrastructure.
By the end of the project the team will have a working prototype that recommends what to learn
next, tracks progress, and schedules revision for each learner, along with an analysis of why each
data structure was chosen.
2.0  Literature Review
Personalized (adaptive) learning has been studied for several decades under the headings of
Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and adaptive hypermedia. Early ITS research showed that tutoring
which adapts to the learner's current knowledge state produces better results than uniform
instruction. Corbett and Anderson's Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (1995) modelled the probability
that a learner has mastered a skill and remains a foundation of many modern systems.
Retention and revision scheduling are supported by Ebbinghaus's forgetting-curve research and by
spaced-repetition methods such as the Leitner box system and the SM-2 algorithm used in
SuperMemo. Modern platforms such as Duolingo have extended this idea with statistical models
(e.g., half-life regression) to decide when an item should be reviewed again.
Commercial platforms such as Khan Academy, Coursera and NPTEL provide large course
catalogues with quizzes and progress dashboards. Most still rely largely on fixed course sequences,
with limited personalization of the learning path. Educational technology literature commonly
represents a curriculum as a concept or prerequisite graph, in which nodes are topics and directed
edges show which topic must be learned before another. Graph algorithms such as BFS, DFS,

topological sorting (Kahn's algorithm) and shortest-path algorithms (Dijkstra) are standard tools for
generating valid learning sequences on such graphs.
Standard DSA textbooks – Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms; Weiss, Data Structures and
Algorithm Analysis; and Sedgewick & Wayne, Algorithms – describe heaps and priority queues for
"best-next" selection, tries for prefix search, balanced trees and hash tables for fast lookup, and the
time-complexity trade-offs of searching and sorting techniques. Online resources such as
GeeksforGeeks, Programiz and the official Python documentation supplement these with
implementation guidance.
Existing status and gap: many published and commercial solutions focus on machine-learning-driven
recommendation, which requires large datasets and heavy computing. There is less material showing
how a personalized learning engine can be built using only core DSA concepts with clear, analysable
complexity. This project fills that gap by designing a transparent, lightweight platform in which
every feature is mapped to a specific data structure or algorithm and evaluated for performance.
3.0  Proposed Methodology
The project will be carried out in the following sequence. The flow of the system is: Learner registers
→ Profile created → Goal / topic selected → Prerequisite graph checked → Next unlocked topic
recommended → Lesson and quiz → Score updated → Weak topics pushed to heap and revision
queue → Progress report → Repeat until goal is reached.
1.​ Requirement analysis: define the learner profile (topics known, quiz scores, time spent, goal)
and the feature set – course catalogue, prerequisite-based learning path, adaptive quiz,
weak-topic recommendation, revision scheduler and progress report.
2.​ Data modelling: prepare a sample course dataset (for example a Programming / DSA course
with 30–50 topics), tag each topic with a difficulty level and list its prerequisites; create sample
learner records.
3.​ Design of data structures: select and design the structures listed in the table below and draw
the overall architecture and module diagram.
4.​ Implementation of core modules: code the catalogue (tree), prerequisite graph, learner profile
store, quiz queue, navigation stack and search module.
5.​ Personalization engine: after each quiz, update the learner's topic score; push weak topics into
a max-heap; generate the next topic using topological order restricted to unlocked topics;
schedule revisions with a spaced-repetition queue.
6.​ Integration and interface: combine the modules into a menu-driven / simple GUI application
in Python so that a learner can register, learn, take quizzes and view recommendations.
7.​ Testing: test with different learner types (beginner, average, advanced) and edge cases such as
empty profile, cyclic prerequisites and repeated topics, to check functionality in various
situations.
8.​ Performance evaluation: compare linear vs. binary search and different sorting algorithms on
growing data sizes, record execution time and analyse time and space complexity.
9.​ Documentation and presentation: prepare the project report, results, screenshots and a
demonstration.
